title: Political Parties and Federal Power, 1796–1819
summary: Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and find two Supreme Court cases that shaped the new government. The elections of 1796 and 1800 show the first party divide; two Supreme Court cases, in 1803 and 1819, show how the new federal government's power was tested.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map compares the elections of 1796 and 1800 state by state: a pie on each of the sixteen states shows how its electors voted in the contests between John Adams (Federalist) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican). The 1800 layer is off when the map opens, because the two sets of pies overlap. Two pink squares mark landmark Supreme Court cases that tested the new federal government's power: Marbury v. Madison (1803) in Washington, D.C., and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) in Baltimore.

layers.name: Election of 1796: electors' votes
layers.shows: A pie on each of the 16 states: electors' votes for John Adams (Federalist, orange) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican, blue), with bigger pies for more electors. Each pop-up lists the votes for each main candidate, with the rest grouped as others.
layers.source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth

layers.name: Election of 1800: electors' votes
layers.shows: The same for 1800. Each pop-up lists every candidate's votes and explains the Jefferson–Burr tie and the 12th Amendment, so no question asks for those.
layers.source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth

layers.name: Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819
layers.shows: Pink squares for Marbury v. Madison (1803, Washington, D.C.) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819, Baltimore), labeled with the case name and year. Each pop-up gives the question, the ruling, why it matters and why it's placed there (Why here).

compellingQuestion.en: How did the first political parties divide the country?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo dividieron al país los primeros partidos políticos?

questions.task: Open The sixteen states bookmark. Use the pies and the legend to find which regions mostly voted for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the two-color pies for the split states' numbers.
frontOfClass: Open The sixteen states bookmark.
Open the legend: orange for John Adams, blue for Thomas Jefferson.
Point out that bigger pies mean more electors.
Ask: which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson?
Click one two-color pie and read the 1796 votes line of the pop-up.
Ask: which states split their votes, and how?

steps.es: Abre el marcador The sixteen states (Los dieciséis estados).

steps.en: Use the legend to read the 1796 pies.
steps.es: Usa la leyenda para leer los gráficos circulares de 1796.

steps.en: Click each two-color pie and read its pop-up.
steps.es: Haz clic en cada gráfico de dos colores y lee su ventana emergente.

ask.en: Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson? Which states split their votes, and how?
ask.es: ¿Qué parte del país votó sobre todo por Adams y cuál por Jefferson? ¿Qué estados dividieron sus votos, y cómo?

answer.where: The sixteen states bookmark; Election of 1796: electors' votes layer. Legend: orange = John Adams, blue = Thomas Jefferson; the pop-up names the state. All-orange pies: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont. All-blue: Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee. Two-color pies, from the pop-up's 1796 votes line: Maryland (Adams 7, Jefferson 4), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14, Adams 1), Virginia (Jefferson 20, Adams 1), North Carolina (Jefferson 11, Adams 1).
answer.accept: Adams: New England and the states around New York (New York, New Jersey, Delaware). Jefferson: the South and the West, plus most of Pennsylvania. The four split states named, with Maryland the only split state Adams won.
answer.text: The totals are not on the map: Adams 71, Jefferson 68, so Jefferson, the runner-up, became vice president.

questions.task: Turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies and click each for the numbers; identify the closest state.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796: electors' votes and turn on Election of 1800: electors' votes.
Ask: which states have two-color pies this time?
Click one of them and read the 1800 votes line of the pop-up.
Ask: how did its electors divide, and which state was the closest?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), desactiva Election of 1796 (Elección de 1796) y activa Election of 1800 (Elección de 1800).
Busca los gráficos de dos colores.

steps.en: Click each one and read how its electors divided.
steps.es: Haz clic en cada uno y lee cómo se dividieron sus electores.

ask.en: Which states have two-color pies this time? How did each one's electors divide between Adams and Jefferson? Which state was the closest?
ask.es: ¿Qué estados tienen gráficos de dos colores esta vez? ¿Cómo se dividieron los electores de cada uno entre Adams y Jefferson? ¿Qué estado estuvo más reñido?

answer.where: Election of 1800: electors' votes layer; two-color pies, pop-up 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4). Closest: Maryland, an even split.
answer.text: Totals, not on the map: Jefferson 73, Burr 73, Adams 65. Each elector cast two votes, so the pop-ups also list Burr and Charles C. Pinckney.

questions.task: Compare the two elections by switching between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 in Map layers. Find the state whose whole pie changed color, the states whose shares changed, and describe where each party was strong.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, switch Election of 1796 off and Election of 1800 on, then back, so the class sees the change.
Ask: which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue?
Click that state's pie and read the number of electors in the pop-up title.
Switch the layers again and look at the two-color pies.
Ask: which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change?
Ask: where was each party strong, and where did the two compete?

steps.en: In Map layers, switch between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 (one on, one off).
steps.es: En las capas del mapa, alterna entre Election of 1796 y Election of 1800 (una activada, la otra desactivada).

steps.en: Find the state whose whole pie changed from orange to blue, and click it to read its electors.
steps.es: Busca el estado cuyo gráfico entero cambió de naranja a azul y haz clic en él para leer sus electores.

steps.en: Find the states whose pies changed their shares, and check New England.
steps.es: Busca los estados cuyos gráficos cambiaron sus proporciones y fíjate en Nueva Inglaterra.

ask.en: Which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue, and how many electors did it have? Which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change? Using both maps, where was each party strong and where did the two parties compete?
ask.es: ¿Qué estado cambió todo su gráfico de naranja a azul, y cuántos electores tenía? ¿Qué estados cambiaron las proporciones de su gráfico, y cambió algún estado de Nueva Inglaterra? Con los dos mapas, ¿dónde era fuerte cada partido y dónde competían los dos partidos?

answer.where: Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers, pop-up title (state and number of electors) and votes lines. New York, 12 electors: all Adams in 1796, all Jefferson in 1800. Shares changed: Maryland (Adams 7–4 to 5–5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14–1 to 8–7), North Carolina (Jefferson 11–1 to 8–4), Virginia (Jefferson 20–1 to 21–0). No New England state changed: Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont stayed all orange.
answer.accept: Names New York as the only state that switched entirely; notes that the middle states (Maryland, Pennsylvania, North Carolina) were split in both elections; says the Federalists were strong in New England and the Democratic-Republicans in the South and West, with the middle states (and New York) deciding the result.
answer.text: New York's 12 votes were more than the margin: without that switch Adams would have had 77 votes to Jefferson's 61 in 1800, instead of 65 to 73.

title.en: The Supreme Court, near the capital
title.es: La Corte Suprema, cerca de la capital

questions.task: Click the two pink squares and read Why here to find what happened in each place; measure the straight-line distance between them and ask why both cases arose so close to the capital.
frontOfClass: Zoom in on the two pink squares near the capital.
Click Marbury v. Madison (1803) and read the Why here part of the pop-up.
Click McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and read its Why here part.
Ask: what happened in each place to bring the case to the Court?
Open Measure and click from one square to the other for the straight-line distance in miles.
Ask: why might both cases have come from so near the capital?

steps.en: Click the two pink squares: Marbury v. Madison (1803) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
steps.es: Haz clic en los dos cuadrados rosados: Marbury v. Madison (1803) y McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).

steps.en: Read the Why here part of each pop-up.
steps.es: Lee la parte Why here (por qué aquí) de cada ventana emergente.

steps.en: Use Measure to find the straight-line distance between the two squares.
steps.es: Usa la herramienta de medir (Measure) para hallar la distancia en línea recta entre los dos cuadrados.

ask.en: What happened in each place to bring the case to the Court? How far apart are the two squares? Why might both cases have come from so near the national capital?
ask.es: ¿Qué ocurrió en cada lugar para que el caso llegara a la Corte? ¿A qué distancia están los dos cuadrados? ¿Por qué crees que los dos casos surgieron tan cerca de la capital nacional?

fill.en: Distance between the two cases: about ____ miles.
fill.es: Distancia entre los dos casos: unas ____ millas.

answer.where: Landmark Supreme Court cases layer. Marbury v. Madison pop-up, Why here: William Marbury asked the Supreme Court in Washington for an order to get his commission. McCulloch v. Maryland pop-up, Why here: Maryland sued James McCulloch, cashier at the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States, to collect its tax on the bank. Measure tool, Baltimore square to Washington square: about 35 miles (accept 32 to 38).
answer.accept: Any sensible link between the places and federal power: the Court and the federal government sat in Washington, so a dispute over a federal appointment began there; the Bank of the United States had a branch in nearby Baltimore, and Maryland's tax on it set state law against federal law.
answer.text: The pop-ups also give the ruling and Why it matters: Marbury established judicial review (the pop-up quotes "A Law repugnant to the Constitution is void"); McCulloch held that Congress could charter the bank and that federal law is supreme over state law, so Maryland's tax was void. Marbury grew out of the change of party in 1801: Marbury was one of John Adams's last-minute appointments, and Jefferson's administration did not deliver his commission.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch that marks each party's region (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or sketch pins for the First Bank of the United States (Philadelphia, 1791) and Washington's Farewell Address (published in Philadelphia, 1796), with notes. Accept answers that name a region for each party, use the split states or New York's switch as evidence, and connect the parties to a dispute over federal power (the bank, the courts).

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 layer to describe which regions voted mostly for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the split states for their numbers.
Switch between the 1796 and 1800 layers to find the state whose whole pie changed color and the states whose shares changed.
Read the two-color pies in the Election of 1800 layer to identify the closest state.
Click the two Supreme Court case markers, read what happened in each place, and measure the straight-line distance between them.
Use the pattern of electors' votes across the sixteen states as evidence to describe where each party was strong in 1800.
discussion: Comparing the 1796 and 1800 pies, where did the Federalists hold on and where did they lose ground? What do those regions have in common on the map?
In both elections a few states split their electors between the two candidates. Which states were they, and why might a state's electors not all vote the same way?

Marbury v. Madison and McCulloch v. Maryland both arose within a short distance of the capital. Using the distance you measured, why might the earliest tests of federal power have come from so close to Washington?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 from the front with the legend open, and write the two candidates and their colors on the board before pairs click the split states.
differentiation.stretch: Using both election layers and the electors in each pop-up title, work out which states Adams would have needed to win in 1800, and what New York's switch was worth.

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers (orange for Adams, blue for Jefferson) with numbers from the pop-up votes lines, such as New York's 12 electors switching from all Adams to all Jefferson, Maryland 7–4 then 5–5 and Pennsylvania 14–1 then 8–7, and the Why here parts of the Supreme Court pop-ups with a Measure distance of about 35 miles.
assessment.exemplar: The first political parties divided the country by region: the Federalists held New England and the Democratic-Republicans held the South and the West, while the middle states were split and decided the result. In the Election of 1796 layer, the legend shows orange for John Adams and blue for Thomas Jefferson, and the pies for Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont are all orange, while Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina and Tennessee are blue. The two-color pies are in the middle: the pop-up's 1796 votes line gives Maryland Adams 7, Jefferson 4, and Pennsylvania Jefferson 14, Adams 1. When I turned on the Election of 1800 layer, New York's whole pie changed from orange to blue, and its pop-up title shows 12 electors, more than the margin, so one state changed who won. Maryland's pop-up shows 5 to 5, the closest state, and Pennsylvania moved to 8 to 7, so the middle stayed contested while no New England state changed. The Landmark Supreme Court cases layer shows the divide went beyond elections: Why here says Marbury asked the Court in Washington for his commission and Maryland taxed the Bank's Baltimore branch, and Measure gives about 35 miles between the squares, so the first fights over federal power were next to the capital. The pattern held in both elections, but the parties only competed in a few states, so most states were not divided inside.

beforeYouStart.en: George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.
beforeYouStart.es: George Washington no pertenecía a ningún partido y, en 1796, cuando se preparaba para dejar la presidencia, advirtió a los estadounidenses contra los partidos. Para entonces ya se habían formado dos: los federalistas, encabezados por John Adams y Alexander Hamilton, y los demócrata-republicanos, encabezados por Thomas Jefferson y James Madison. Cada elector emitía dos votos para presidente, y quien quedaba en segundo lugar era vicepresidente.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; each pop-up has a Why here part. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en un gráfico circular para ver el nombre del estado y su número de electores. Cada gráfico muestra cómo votaron los electores de un estado: naranja para John Adams (federalista) y azul para Thomas Jefferson (demócrata-republicano); usa la leyenda. Los gráficos más grandes indican más electores. Cada elector emitía dos votos; la ventana emergente muestra a los demás candidatos. La capa Election of 1800 está desactivada al abrir el mapa. Los cuadrados rosados marcan dos casos de la Corte Suprema; cada ventana emergente tiene una parte Why here (por qué aquí). Maine aparece dentro de Massachusetts y Virginia Occidental dentro de Virginia, y no se muestran los territorios.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the first political parties that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre los primeros partidos políticos que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: When the map opens, Election of 1796 and the Supreme Court layer are on and Election of 1800 is off, because the two sets of pie charts overlap. Students switch between the two elections in Map layers for questions 2 and 3.

misconceptions.response: Electors did, and states chose their electors in different ways. In 1796 and 1800 each elector cast two votes.
They were rivals from different parties: in 1796 Jefferson, the runner-up, became Adams's vice president.

misconceptions.claim: The 1800 tie was between Jefferson and Adams.
misconceptions.response: It was between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, with 73 votes each.

standards.text: Explain the origin and development of American political parties
Identify the origin of judicial review
Summarize the issues, decisions, and significance of landmark Supreme Court cases, including Marbury v. Madison, McCulloch v. Maryland, and Gibbons v. Ogden
Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of John Adams's presidency.
Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of Thomas Jefferson's presidency.
Explain the powers and limits of the three branches of government, public officials, and bureaucracies at different levels in the United States and in other countries.
